title: Migration Dynamics and Quality of Life Index
text:
2.1 Data Source
The datasets used in the project are:
1.Population size of the provinces
2.Migration received by provinces according to the reason for migration
3.Migration rates by provinces according to the reason for migration
4.[Net migration rate for provinces according to reasons for migration] Calculated as “Migration Outgoing - Migration Incoming”
5.Life Index Rankings and Index Values by Province
In this study, the five datasets mentioned above were used, graphs were plotted, and the results were thoroughly analyzed.

title: Migration Dynamics and Quality of Life Index
text:
2.2 General Information About Data
Our dataset tracks migration metrics across all 81 provinces of Turkiye from 2018 to 2024. It combines raw inbound/outbound migration figures with detailed columns explaining 12 different reasons for migration, cross-references them with the Turkish Statistical Institute’s (TUIK) comprehensive Life Index scores, and shows the relationships between them.

title: Migration Dynamics and Quality of Life Index
text:
2.3 Reason of Choice
We chose this data because migration cannot be explained solely by economic factors. By combining net migration metrics with the multidimensional Life Index (which assesses health, education, security, and environment), we can reveal the relationship between internal migration in Turkiye and life indices.

title: Migration Dynamics and Quality of Life Index

Code
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

yedek_veri <- VerilenGoc
orijinal_isimler <- colnames(yedek_veri)

# 1. Sutun isimlerini R'in hata vermeyecegi guvenli kodlara ceviriyoruz
colnames(yedek_veri) <- c("Yil", "Il", "Toplam_Miktar", paste0("Neden_", 1:(ncol(yedek_veri) - 3)))

# 2. Sadece Turkiye geneli satirlarini filtreliyoruz
toplam_verisi <- yedek_veri[yedek_veri$Il == "Toplam-Total", ]

yillar <- sort(unique(toplam_verisi$Yil))
top3_verisi <- data.frame()

# 3. Her yil icin en buyuk ilk 3 nedeni dongu ile ayikliyoruz
for(y in yillar) {
  satir <- toplam_verisi[toplam_verisi$Yil == y, ]
  rakamlar <- as.numeric(satir[1, 4:ncol(satir)])
  
  # Buyukten kucuge siralayip ilk 3 indeks numarasini aliyoruz
  sirali_indeksler <- order(rakamlar, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
  
  for(i in 1:3) {
    idx <- sirali_indeksler[i]
    neden_metni <- orijinal_isimler[idx + 3]
    neden_metni <- gsub("\\r\\n.*", "", neden_metni) # Gizli karakter temizligi
    
    top3_verisi <- rbind(
      top3_verisi,
      data.frame(
        Yil = y,
        Sira = paste0(i, "."), # 1. 2. ve 3. ibaresi
        Goc_Nedeni = neden_metni,
        Kisi_Bin = rakamlar[idx] / 1000
      )
    )
  }
}

# 4. ESTETIK VE SIRALI COKLU PANEL GRAFIGINI CIZIYORUZ
ggplot(top3_verisi, aes(x = Sira, y = Kisi_Bin, fill = Goc_Nedeni)) +
  # Sutunlarimizi olusturuyoruz
  geom_col(width = 0.7, alpha = 0.9) +
  
  # Sutunlarin uzerine net bin kisi degerlerini yaziyoruz
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(Kisi_Bin, 1)),
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 2.8,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  
  # Grafigi yillara gore yan yana panellere boluyoruz
  facet_wrap(~Yil, nrow = 1) +
  
  # Akademik ve net renk paleti
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  
  # Minimalist arka plan temasi
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  labs(
    title = "Yillara Gore En Yuksek Ilk 3 Goc Verme Nedeni (2018-2024)",
    subtitle = "Her yilin kendi icinde en buyuk 1. 2. ve 3. gerekcelerinin karsilastirmasi",
    x = "Neden Siralamasi",
    y = "Kisi Sayisi (Bin Kisi)",
    fill = "Goc Etme Gerekceleri"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13, color = "#2c3e50"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, face = "italic", color = "gray40"),
    # Uzun aciklamalar alt alta temiz dursun diye lejanti alta aliyoruz
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    # Yil basliklarinin kutularini makale stilinde susluyoruz
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f1f3f5", color = NA),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10, color = "#2c3e50")
  ) +
  # Uzun cumlelerin tasmamasi icin aciklamalari tekli sutun yapiyoruz
  guides(fill = guide_legend(ncol = 1))











Code
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# 1. Veriyi hazırla ve filtrele (Sütun ismi yerine indeks numarası kullanıyoruz)
neden_verisi_2024 <- VerilenGoc %>%
  # 1. sütun Yıl (2024) ve 2. sütun İl (Toplam-Total) olan satırı seçiyoruz
  filter(.[[1]] == 2024 & .[[2]] == "Toplam-Total") %>%
  # İlk 3 sabit sütunu (Yıl, İl, Toplam) indeks numaralarıyla tablodan çıkarıyoruz
  select(-c(1, 2, 3)) %>% 
  # Tabloyu ggplot'un anlayacağı uzun (long) formata çeviriyoruz
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Goc_Nedeni", values_to = "Kisi_Sayisi") %>%
  mutate(Kisi_Sayisi_Bin = Kisi_Sayisi / 1000)

# Sütun isimlerindeki o sorun çıkaran \r\n karakterlerini temizliyoruz
neden_verisi_2024$Goc_Nedeni <- gsub("\\r\\n.*", "", neden_verisi_2024$Goc_Nedeni) 

# 2. Grafiği Çiz (İller grafiğindeki sıkışma olmasın diye yazı boyutunu da ayarladık)
ggplot(neden_verisi_2024, aes(x = Kisi_Sayisi_Bin, y = reorder(Goc_Nedeni, Kisi_Sayisi_Bin))) +
  geom_col(fill = "forestgreen", alpha = 0.8) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "2024 Yili Goc Nedenleri",
    x = "Kisi Sayısı (Bin Kisi)",
    y = "Goc Etme Gerekcesi"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9), # Gerekçelerin yazı boyutu
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank() # Yatay kalabalık çizgileri gizler
  )









If we look at the most recent data from 2024, we see that the main reasons for migration are family-based migration and the pursuit of better living conditions and education. The highest value for 2024 actually shows us that the population living in Turkey is family-oriented, which is not surprising. Second, we see that people are relocating in large numbers in search of better living conditions. Third, regarding education, we see that the factors of university and school continue to be among the foundations of internal migration in Turkiye.

If we examine migration trends between 2018 and 2024, we see that the lowest figure was recorded in 2020, the year of the pandemic. We can say that the curfews and prevailing uncertainty during that period may have prevented people from moving away from the cities where they lived. We also see that the highest increase occurred in 2023, as the Kahramanmaras earthquake struck in February 2023, prompting people to begin migrating to safer cities with lower earthquake risks. We also see a relatively high migration trend in 2018. During that period, due to the economic crisis and inflation in Turkiye, there was a migration trend from expensive metropolitan cities like Ankara and Istanbul to smaller cities.

title: Migration Dynamics and Quality of Life Index
text:
3.2 Trend Analysis
The graph shows the relational analysis between migration rate data and life indices of the provinces.


Code
yasam_df <- read_excel("C:/emu660-spring2026-burcubaris/YasamEndeksi.xlsx", col_names = TRUE)
goc_df <- read_excel("C:/emu660-spring2026-burcubaris/Gochizi.xlsx", col_names = TRUE)

colnames(yasam_df)[1:2] <- c("Il", "Endeks")
colnames(goc_df)[1:3]   <- c("Yil", "Il", "Goc")

goc_2024 <- subset(goc_df, Yil == 2024 & Il != "Toplam-Total")

veri_seti <- inner_join(yasam_df, goc_2024, by = "Il")

grafik <- ggplot(veri_seti, aes(x = Endeks, y = Goc, label = Il)) + 
  geom_point(color = "#1f77b4", size = 3, alpha = 0.7) + 
  geom_text_repel(size = 3, max.overlaps = 15) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red", se = TRUE, formula = y ~ x) + 
  labs(
    title = "Il Yasam Endeksi ve 2024 Net Goc Hizi İliskisi",
    x = "Genel Yasam Endeksi",
    y = "Net Goc Hizi (‰)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

print(grafik)

title: Migration Dynamics and Quality of Life Index
text:
3.3 Results
When we examine the graph, we see a positive correlation between the overall quality of life index and the net migration rate. It has been observed that provinces with a high quality of life index tend to attract more migration, while those with a low index tend to lose population. Developed provinces such as Istanbul, Ankara, Antalya, and Muğla have a positive net migration rate, while provinces such as Ağrı, Muş, Şırnak, and Kars stand out with negative net migration rates. However, the fact that the data points do not cluster entirely around the regression line indicates that migration patterns cannot be explained solely by the quality of life index and that other economic, social, and demographic factors also play a role.

section: (a) A brief summary about “Veri Bilimi ve Endüstri Mühendisliği Üzerine Sohbetler - Baykal Hafızoğlu & Erdi Daşdemir” video:
text:
(a) A brief summary about “Veri Bilimi ve Endüstri Mühendisliği Üzerine Sohbetler - Baykal Hafızoğlu & Erdi Daşdemir” video:
Our lecturer Dr. Erdi Daşdemir’s guest Baykal Hafızoğlu talks about operation research (OR) and data science. Defining himself as an OR and Optimization Scientist, Mr. Hafızoğlu explains that his core mission involves the formulation and resolution of complex mathematical models to address real-world challenges.
Mr. Hafızoğlu notes that the traditional definition of OR has changed a lot over the past few years. He argues that while it used to be related to optimization and statistics, it is now more closely associated with artificial intelligence and machine learning. For this reason, Mr. Hafızoğlu prefers to refer OR as an “analytics”. He categorizes analytics into four topic and shows these topics as a graphic: Descriptive, Diagnostic, Predictive  and Prescriptive analytics.
Later in his speech, he talks about his own experiences. He says, “All projects begin with a clear problem definition.” He explains that the problem definition must be clear and concise, even when dealing with the simplest of matters. This is the most important thing.
Mr. Hafızoğlu notes that one of the most important things is to truly understand the user. An early-stage prototype should be presented to the customer without delay, and feedback should be gathered. The user should not struggle to understand the user interface. It is really important that users understand and adopt the model they will be using. This is because users do not want to use models they do not understand. Therefore, we must be able to explain the analytical model we have created.
Finally, he answers the questions of undergraduate students to satisfy their curiosity.

title: Assignment 1
text:
(b) Open-ended and Multiple-Choice Questions
b.1. Open-ended Question
Based on the value and complexity graph shown at the 26:45 -minute mark of the video, please explain how analytics evolves from descriptive analytics to prescriptive analytics. What changes in terms of the type of questions answered and the value created for decision making?
** Answer **
As analytics progresses from descriptive to prescriptive analytics, both the complexity of methods and the value generated for decision making increase. Descriptive analytics focuses on understanding what happened in the past using techniques such as data visualization and time series analysis. Diagnostic analytics goes further by analyzing why something happened. Predictive analytics uses methods like regression, simulation, and machine learning to estimate what is likely to happen in the future. Finally, prescriptive analytics recommends the best actions by using optimization, heuristics, and mathematical modeling to support decision making.
b.2. Multiple-Choice Question
According to the figure, what is the main difference between predictive analytics and prescriptive analytics?
A) Predictive analytics focuses on describing past data, while prescriptive analytics focuses on visualizing data.
B) Predictive analytics estimates what is likely to happen, while prescriptive analytics recommends what actions should be taken.
C) Predictive analytics only uses machine learning, while prescriptive analytics only uses statistics.
D) Predictive analytics focuses on historical reports, while prescriptive analytics focuses only on data storage.
Correct Answer: B

compute_stats <- function(x) {
  
  stats <- list(
    mean = mean(x),
    median = median(x),
    variance = var(x),
    IQR = IQR(x),
    min = min(x),
    max = max(x)
  )
  
  return(stats)
}


for(col in names(mtcars)) {
  
  cat("Column:", col, "\n")
  
  result <- compute_stats(mtcars[[col]])
  
  print(result)
  
  cat("\n")
}
